results.message: What was a sermon like at Hippo?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
A sermon at Hippo was the man in charge of you, speaking to your face, again and again. You were there in the room, baptized or still learning, and the same voice worked on you week after week. It was not a lecture and not a show. It was the bishop answerable for your life, telling you what he thought you needed.

Augustine said it himself: “You share communion with the members of the Apostles. You share communion with the shrines of the holy martyrs, who are spread over the whole world. And you belong to my care, so that I may give a good account of you. You know what my whole account is. ‘Lord, You know that I have spoken. You know that I have not kept silent. You know in what spirit I have spoken. You know that I have wept before You when I spoke and was not heard.’”

The charge ran both ways. He answered for his flock, and his flock could stand in front of his seat and refuse to leave until he heard them. The people put him there, loudly, and he wept. That is who stood to listen when he preached.

Preaching was the main way what we held reached an ordinary believer. It was not one force among several. It was how the office itself worked.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

glosses.plain_meaning: We are not a silent audience. We put men into office, and we say so out loud. We can stand in front of a bishop's own seat and refuse to go home.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, 'the people' names the congregation when it acts. They consent, they demand, and they elect -- unlike the flock, which is the congregation being cared for.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a passive congregation or a modern democratic electorate with formal voting rights. Neither is right. A corporate body whose consent and demand genuinely constitute a call to office, and which can be exerted disruptively, but which holds no procedural mechanism and can still be refused.
false_friend: a passive congregation with no real leverage over its own clergy
a modern democratic electorate, with a formal ballot and a fixed voting procedure

glosses.plain_meaning: You are in the room, baptized or still learning. Again and again, the same voice works on you. It is not a lecture and not a show. It is the man in charge of you, telling you to your face what he thinks you need.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, preaching is the regular talk to the whole church, baptized or still learning. It is the main way what we hold reaches an ordinary believer.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a stern moralizing monologue or a polished performance piece, and assume it is one component of a service among several. For us it was the central formative act of ordinary life, delivered by the person personally answerable for the hearers, occasional and responsive rather than scripted, and openly aware of what it competed with for people's own attention.
false_friend: a stern moralizing monologue, or a polished performance piece, assumed to be one component of a service among several rather than the central formative act

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

confidence.divergence_note: In the vendored English edition of Cyprian the Latin plebs occurs exactly three times, all inside the 19th-century American editor's own introductory and elucidatory prose, none inside Cyprian's own letters. Cyprian's Latin does use it: Hartel's letters carry plebs in running text, 89 whole-word occurrences with notes excluded, and letter 43 is headed CYPRIANVS PLEBI VNIVERSAE S. 'The people' is the English volume's own recurring rendering for the congregation as an acting body. It is a working handle, and whether plebs becomes the world word is not settled.

Down-tiered from Doc_03's own Tier 1 proposal, which rested on raw frequency (119 occurrences of 'preach' within the Sermons alone). Doc_05 SS5.2's own ecological finding is that this gravity functions as the medium the other gravities are taught and enforced through, not as an independently organizing force -- raw frequency measured the volume of the channel, not the weight of what it carries.
